A sirocco is a powerful, hot wind that blows out of the Sahara Desert in North Africa and travels northward across the Mediterranean Sea toward southern Europe.
What exactly is it?

Think of it this way: the Sahara Desert is one of the hottest, driest places on Earth. Sometimes, weather systems pull massive amounts of air up from that desert and push it northward. That moving mass of extremely hot, dry, dust-laden desert air is a sirocco.

It isn't just a gentle breeze. It's a large-scale meteorological event — a sustained wind that can last for hours or even days.
Where does it come from, and where does it go?

It begins over the Sahara and the Arabian deserts, then sweeps northward and northwestward. Its path takes it over North Africa first (countries like Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco), and then it crosses the Mediterranean Sea before hitting southern Europe — especially southern Italy, Sicily, Malta, Sardinia, and sometimes Greece and Spain.
What does it carry?

When a sirocco is born over the desert, it picks up fine sand and dust particles. These get carried for thousands of kilometres. This is why, during a sirocco, the sky can turn a hazy yellowish or reddish colour, the air looks murky, and a thin layer of reddish dust from the Sahara can settle on cars, windows, and surfaces across southern Europe. People in Rome or Palermo sometimes wake up to find their cars dusted in orange Saharan sand — that's the sirocco at work.
How does it change as it travels?

This is an important and fascinating detail. The sirocco starts dry, because it comes from a desert. But as it passes over the Mediterranean Sea, it picks up moisture from the water below. So:

  • In North Africa: it feels searingly hot and bone-dry, almost like opening a hot oven and standing in front of it. It can rapidly desiccate (dry out) vegetation, soil, and anything exposed to it.
  • By the time it reaches southern Europe: it has absorbed sea moisture and can feel hot and oppressively humid at the same time — sticky, suffocating, and exhausting. This combination of heat and humidity is widely considered even more unpleasant than dry heat alone.
What does it feel like to be in one?

People who have experienced a sirocco often describe it as deeply unpleasant and draining. The key qualities are:

  • Intense heat — temperatures can rise sharply and unusually, far above seasonal norms
  • Dust and poor visibility — the air feels gritty; your eyes, nose, and throat can become irritated
  • A heavy, oppressive atmosphere — breathing feels harder, and the heat has a physical weight to it
  • Psychological effect — historically, people living in Mediterranean regions have attributed irritability, fatigue, low mood, headaches, and even anxiety to the sirocco. Whether or not it truly affects brain chemistry, the discomfort it brings is real, and there is a long cultural tradition of blaming the sirocco for people feeling "off." Some legal traditions in southern Italy once reportedly considered sirocco-induced stress as a mitigating factor in crimes of passion — that is how seriously this wind was taken.
How strong can it get?

It can range from a persistent uncomfortable warmth to gale-force winds. In extreme cases, it can cause sandstorms in North Africa and severely reduced visibility. It has been known to damage crops and stress livestock. When it reaches Europe, its force is often somewhat reduced, but it can still blow strongly enough to be dangerous.
What are the other names for the same (or very similar) winds?

The sirocco goes by many local names across the region. In Libya it's called the ghibli; in Egypt and the Middle East, the khamsin (a word meaning "fifty," because it was believed to blow for about fifty days in spring); in Morocco it's the chergui. In Italy itself, the more common spelling is scirocco. These are all names for essentially the same type of phenomenon — a hot, dusty wind born in the desert and moving toward the sea and Europe. The word "sirocco" in English is the most widely recognised umbrella term for all of them.
When does it happen?

Siroccos are most common in spring (roughly March through May) and to a lesser extent in autumn. Spring is the peak season because that's when certain pressure patterns over the Sahara most reliably generate the conditions needed to push hot desert air northward.
Can the word be used figuratively?

Yes, occasionally. In writing or speech, "sirocco" can be used metaphorically to describe anything that feels like an overwhelming, scorching, suffocating force — something that arrives suddenly, brings intense heat (literal or metaphorical), and leaves you drained. For example, a writer might describe a sudden rush of criticism or a punishing workload as "a sirocco of pressure." This figurative use is relatively uncommon, but it exists.
The one-sentence summary

A sirocco is a hot, dry, dust-carrying wind that originates in the Sahara Desert and sweeps northward across the Mediterranean, bringing intense heat, haze, and oppressive humidity to North Africa and southern Europe — and historically, to the tempers and moods of everyone in its path.
